title: Longer Than
statement: This series was made in a single day, on a short spring climb up Ještěd, a mountain wrapped in thick fog. Objects ahead slowly emerged from the whiteness, while those behind slowly dissolved back into it. That movement became, for me, a precise model of how memory works.

The idea that memory does not store the past but reconstructs it has long been shared by philosophy and psychology alike. As early as 1932, Frederic Bartlett showed that remembering is not reproduction but construction. Maurice Halbwachs wrote that the past is rebuilt each time within the frameworks of the present. Paul Ricœur described memory as the presence of the absent — an image of something that no longer exists, yet still lays claim to faithfulness. Contemporary neuroscience adds that every time a memory is recalled, it becomes open to change.

The fog on Ještěd made this process visible. The photographs sit on the threshold between appearing and disappearing — where it is no longer possible to tell with certainty what really was, and what has been filled in by how we relate to it now.
The series exists as a handmade photobook, published in a small edition.

lines: It erases the world little by little.
Then the belief that you ever knew this place as it was.
At some point only a sensation remains.
Memory keeps not events but traces of them.
